GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
1 
Growth Experiments of Pisum Sativum ‘Sugar Bon’ in Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant 
Laura E. Campbell

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
2 
Growth Experiments of Pisum Sativum ‘Sugar Bon’ in Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant 
Creating a closed-loop lunar habitat system requires maximizing the use native resources 
while using consumable materials that are renewable or recyclable within the system and create 
minimum waste. The weight and volume of materials (payload) that must be carried from Earth 
to the surface of the moon to set-up a closed-loop system are constrained per trip, so using 
materials that can be grown or renewed is also desirable from a transportation efficiency 
perspective. Specific to food and nutrition sub-systems, the lunar regolith can be used as a base 
medium for growing food, but is completely inorganic and lacks several nutrients essential to 
plant growth and must be amended to successfully grow enough to feed lunar inhabitants. 
These experiments tested four renewable (growable) amendments, each targeted at 
specific “soil” improvements: plant nutrition, improved nutrient absorption, and improved 
texture. The four amendments tested were common hypnum moss, spirulina algae, a 
mycorrhizal fungi blend, and a rhizobium bacteria blend targeted to the plant used in these 
experiments, Pisum Sativum ‘Sugar Bon’, or Sugar Bon Snap Peas. Sugar Bon Snap Peas were 
selected because they are a legume, known for the unique symbiotic relationship created with 
specific nitrogen-fixing rhizobia, and for their compact, determinate growth habit and fast 
maturation rate, as these experiments were conducted over a 70-day period with a limited 
amount of lunar regolith simulant allowed. 
Two sets of growing mediums were tested. Several attempts to germinate pea seeds were 
mostly unsuccessful using the first set of growing mediums. On Day 25, the first growing 
mediums were deemed unviable and replaced with mediums composed of different amendment 
proportions, with the exception of a plain regolith medium that did have germination success. 
The second set of growing mediums were used Day 27 through Day 70.

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
7 
 
Materials, Measurements, and Methods 
Growing Environment 
The growing station was a coated steel shelving unit measuring 33.5”x21.625”x74.75” 
with two 13.5”x22.25” 4-bulb fluorescent light fixtures initially set at a 13” clearance above the 
primary grow shelf. The light fixtures can be raised to provide additional clearance, if needed. 
Each light fixture contains two alternating blue (6500K) and red (3000K) 2500-lumen grow 
lights for a total of eight lights. The front and back of the shelves are covered with Mylar sheets 
to improve light retention. The front sheet can be rolled up to allow access to the plants when 
needed. The shelf was kept at room temperature. An 8” fan was set up on one end to blow 
across the grow shelf to provide air flow, cooling, and improve stalk strength and pollination. 
The lights and fan were on an automatic 24-hour timed cycle of 18 hours on and 6 hours off. 
Observing the plants’ root systems was important in this experiment, so the growing 
containers selected were transparent, 32 oz food grade containers with a single ∅.25” drainage 
hole hot-pressed at bottom center. The lids were used as a drip trays to catch excess water. 
Water was not restricted and was given as needed based on measurements and 
observations. Only commercially obtained distilled water was used.

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
8 
 
Selected Crop Seed - Sugar Bon Snap Peas 
The seeds selected for these growth experiments were untreated Sugar Bon Snap Pea 
seeds commercially purchased from the Burpee seed company. Peas were selected because 
they are self-fertile and a popular edible member of the legume family. 'Sugar Bon’ Snap Peas 
were specifically selected because the plants stay small, growing to 18-24 inches tall in normal 
conditions, and they mature quickly, producing edible pods in approximately 56 days. 
 
Lunar Regolith Simulant 
The lunar regolith simulant used in these experiments was commercially-obtained LHS-
1 simulant from the University of Central Florida’s CLASS Exolith Laboratory. 
 
Rhizobium Bacteria Strains Used 
Commercially obtained ‘Verdesian GUARD-N’ rhizobium bacteria was introduced to all 
plants at several times throughout the experimental timeframe in an attempt to initiate the 
nitrogen-fixing process in the peas’ root systems. This commercial blend is specifically targeted 
at legumes including peas and contains the dry bacteria strains Bradyrhizobium sp. (Vigna), 
Bradyrhizobium japonium, Rhizobium leguminosarum biovar phaseoli, and Rhizobium 
leguminosarum biovar viceae. 
 
Mycorrhizal Fungi Strains Used 
Commercially obtained ‘Wildroot Organic Mycorrhizal Concentrate’ was introduced to 
half of the plants at several times throughout the experimental timeframe in an attempt to initiate 
a secondary symbiotic relationship in the peas’ root systems. The intent was to evaluate if the 
presence of mycorrhizal microbials would influence the formation of the rhizobium root colonies 
or the general uptake of nutrients in the pea plants, in general. This commercial blend contains 
the dry endomycorrhizal fungi spores Glomus intradices, Glomus mosseae, Glomus aggregatum, 
Glomus etunicatum, Glomus monosporum, Glomus deserticola, Glomus clarum, Paraglomus 
brasiliannum, and Gigaspora margarita. This blend also contains spores of several 
ectomycorrhizal fungi that do not contribute to the experiment.

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
9 
Hypnum Moss Amendment 
A common hypnum moss was selected as one of the primary regolith amendments for 
several reasons. Moss provides water retention, aeriation, and “fluffiness” to the planting 
mediums. Considering transportation efficiency, moss is an additive that can be grown on site 
with very little input, doubling its biomass in six months. Moss absorbs water and nutrients from 
the air, uses light to make its own food, and can anchor on a variety of surfaces. Its addition to 
an existing growing system can be made opportunistic, i.e., little special input for high output 
and benefit. 
The moss used in these experiments was obtained by scraping and lifting wild patches 
from compacted clay, then rinsing the patches under running tap water to remove clay residue 
until the water ran clean when the moss was squeezed. Foreign material (rocks and organic 
debris) was handpicked out, and then the clean moss sheets were dried at 200°F in an oven. The 
nutrient and microbial contamination from the clay the moss grew on was deemed acceptable for 
these initial experiments. 
 
Spirulina Algae Amendment 
Spirulina Algae (Arthrospira platensis) was also selected as a regolith amendment as a 
source of plant nutrition. Unlike the moss, a specific growing system would be required to grow 
Spirulina. However, there are several publications and articles boasting of Spirulina being 
evaluated by NASA for a variety of human nutrition and bio fuel applications on future space 
exploration missions. Providing complete nutrition plants is yet another potential application. 
The spirulina used in these experiments was a commercially obtained fresh paste, air 
dried at room temperature over several days, mechanically ground, then filtered thru a standard 
18x16 aluminum screen to remove larger particles. 
 
Measurements Taken 
Temperature, humidity, and dew point measurements were recorded automatically 
every hour using a blue “Tempo Disc”. 
Other observations and manual measurements were made daily when possible. The 
following measurements were taken regularly:

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
10 
1. Medium moisture was measured with a generic moisture probe and recorded before 
and after any water was added. 
2. Water usage was recorded as it was consumed. Each plant container was assigned 
its own container of distilled water so consumption could be easily monitored and 
measured. Water used was recorded to the nearest 10mL. 
3. Soil pH measurements were taken using a “Rapitest” digital soil pH meter probe. 
4. The number of sprouts, flower buds, fruit, lost bud/fruit were counted and recorded 
when observed. 
5. Plant height, visible root depth, and fruit length were measured with a standard inch 
ruler. 
 
Medium Distribution and Experimental Preparation and Environment 
Two sets of growing mediums were tested. The first set of growing mediums were tested 
Day 1 through Day 27. Seeds did not germinate in the amended regolith simulant after several 
attempts. New regolith simulant was obtained and a new set of mediums with different 
amendment proportions was mixed. The second set of growing mediums were used Day 27 
through Day 70. The original control samples, using Earth dirt and unamended regolith simulant, 
were maintained and were not restarted with the second set. 
Each container of medium began with four seeds. In each trial, one seed was planted at 
the side of each container and the location was marked with an arrow so that the maturation of 
this seed might be viewed through the side of the container. The remaining three seeds were 
equally spaced around the middle of each container. Seeds were pushed down approximately 
one inch deep into the mediums then watered. Sprouted plants were given an identification 
number indexed clock-wise from the side position marked with an arrow, with the plant at the 
side position being #1. 
Seeds in the first two sowings were soaked overnight and inoculated by coating before 
planting. Because few of those seeds germinated, seeds in subsequent plantings were not soaked 
or inoculated before planting, but planted dry in order to eliminate seed drowning as the root 
cause of germination failure. In the subsequent plantings, the microbial inoculations were added 
via watering solution at random points through the experimental timeframe.

Second Set of Growing Mediums & Seed Preparation. 
The second set of growing mediums were mixed in the proportions detailed in Figure 4. 
Baseline data and measurements are detailed in Figure 5. Algae concentrations being too high 
were suspected to be the main cause of germination failure and were not added as part of the 
planting mediums in the second attempt. The controls from the first set of growing mediums 
were retained but renumbered. The Earth soil control container was renumbered “#0” and the 
control container with only regolith simulant was renumbered “#1”. Seeds were planted dry and 
were not inoculated. Microbials and algae feedings were added via watering solutions at random 
points through the experimental timeframe.

Theory 
These experiments were designed to study the range of viability of the experimental 
amendments and microbials to determine if additional study was merited for more refined future 
experimentation. Beyond knowledge of articles and publications regarding NASA’s evaluation 
of Spirulina for a variety of other space-based applications, this work is believed to be original 
by the author. No previous research was found on the use of microbials, moss, or algae as lunar 
regolith amendments. 
 
Investigation Topics 
The intent of these experiments was to test 
1) If the peas could complete a life cycle (germinate, mature, flower, and produce seed) 
in mediums that contained between 50% and 100% lunar regolith simulant? 
2) If a symbiotic relationship between the peas and the rhizobium could be established 
in mediums that contained between 50% and 100% lunar regolith simulant? 
3) If the symbiotic relationship between the peas and the mycorrhizal fungi could be 
established in mediums that contained between 50% and 100% lunar regolith 
simulant? 
4) If both of these symbiotic relationships could be established, was there any noticeable 
additional benefit or impairment to the plants? 
5) If hypnum moss as a regolith amendment was effective for the purposes of water 
retention, aeration, and root spread? 
6) If Spirulina algae is effective as a plant food. 
 
Expectations & Hypotheses 
Effectiveness of Spirulina. 
Some pretesting of reconstituting the Spirulina led to a prediction that using too much 
would cause the mediums to become too gummy and interfere with soil aeriation. Because of 
this pretesting, the plants in the lower percentage of spirulina were predicted to do better than 
those in higher percentage during the first trial.

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
18 
Observations during the first trial led to eliminating Spirulina from the medium mixes for 
the second trial. In the second trial, the plants that were allowed to be given Spirulina as a 
nutrition supplement were predicted to be healthier than those that were not. 
Effectiveness of Hypnum moss. 
Seeds planted in the containers with higher moss percentages, in particular, were 
anticipated to do better in the trials as the moss was expected to make the soil fluffy and less 
dense, allowing the roots to spread more easily throughout the container. The comparison of root 
spreading was likely to be observable through the sides of the transparent containers. 
Microbial symbiotic relationships. 
It was predicted that the rhizobium would be able to establish colonies in the pea plant 
roots and improve the health of the plant. These colonies appear as white or pink root nodules on 
the roots. It was hoped these could be observed on the roots through sides of the transparent 
containers. 
It was predicted that the mycorrhizal would establish colonies in mediums that contained 
the hypnum moss. They were not expected to establish in the containers with 100% regolith 
simulant. Even after it was established that the peas would sprout in 100% regolith simulant, 
because the fungi behave similarly to plant roots, they were not expected to establish. 
Seeds planted in 100% regolith simulant. 
Germination was anticipated, but sprouts breaking through to the surface was not 
expected in the initial 100% regolith simulant control sample because of the high soil density. In 
the second trial, the plants in the 100% regolith sample that were allowed to have algae as a 
possible nutrition source were expected to do better than the plants without a nutritional 
supplement. 
Seeds planted in a distribution of Spirulina and hypnum moss with regolith 
simulant. 
Considering all anticipated effects of the soil amendments and microbial inoculations, in 
the first trial, container #6 (5% Spirulina + 35% Moss + Rhizobium + Mycorrhizal Fungi) was 
anticipated to host the healthiest plants. In the second trial, container #10 (45% Moss + 
Rhizobium + Mycorrhizal Fungi + Algae feeding) was anticipated to host the healthiest plants.

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT

planting, no seeds germinated in any of the containers that contained moss or algae. 
Timing of successful seedlings sprouting and growth during Trial #1 is shown in Figure 
10. No plants matured to the point of producing flowers or seeds during Trial #1.

On Day 8, the seeds were removed from containers #2 through #10 and the growing 
mediums were set out to dry overnight. These seeds had mostly rotted and none had radicles that 
had broken through the seed coat. The observation was made that the mediums held water very 
well and too much water was suspected to have drowned the seeds. 
On Day 9, the mediums were returned to the original containers and new seeds were 
soaked, inoculated, and planted. It was observed that removing and churning the mediums 
increased the amount of air incorporation, making the mediums less dense and added over an 
inch of medium depth in each container. This was hoped to improve the number of seeds that 
would successfully sprouts. It did not.

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
20 
On Day 21, seeds in containers #2 through #10 were removed. These seeds had mostly 
rotted again and none had radicles that had broken through the seed coat. Less water had been 
used and the mediums did not need to be dried out. Seed drowning was still suspected as a 
possible root cause of germination failure and new seeds were planted dry without inoculation. 
Seed viability and germination rate was also tested at this point via placing 10 seeds in a 
damp paper towel. 70% of the tested seeds germinated in 3 days. 
On Day 25, seeds were removed from containers #3 through #10 to check for 
germination. None had radicles that had broken through the seed coat. Comparing this result to 
the 70% ‘damp paper towel’ germination rate in a similar period of time, it was decided that the 
root cause of germination failure was likely due to a component in the growing mediums. This 
concluded Trial #1. 
 
Summary of root cause evaluation of germination failure Day 1 through Day 21. 
Four causes of seed germination failure were suspected: 
1. Seed drowning from overwatering 
2. Seed drowning from overnight seed soaking prior to planting 
3. Seed Viability 
4. Use of algae in planting mediums 
5. Use of moss in planting mediums 
The seeds drowning from overwatering was unlikely as water usage was cut back after 
the second sowing on Day 9. The seeds drowning from overnight seed soaking was unlikely as 
the dry seeds sown on Day 21 also did not germinate. Seed viability was tested by placing 
several seeds in a damp paper towel. 70% of the seeds germinated (radicle broke through seed 
coat) after 3 days. Seed viability was eliminated as a root cause. To eliminate the other possible 
root causes, new mediums had to be created and tested. This led to the conclusion of Trial #1.

additional seeds were planted at the side positions in containers #0 and #1. This changed the 
indexing and ID number of existing plants, but was desired to observe growth through the side of 
the container and to monitor growth at the same rate as the new trials. 50%-100% of seeds

Rhizobia Colonies 
During the grow period, no rhizobia were observed through the transparent containers. 
At the conclusion of the grow period, each plant was carefully removed from the growing 
medium so that the roots could be observed. Every plant had rhizobia colonies that had infected 
the root structures. Most colonies were towards the surface of the growing medium. Figure 14 
shows pictures taken of the rhizobia colonies observed.

Mycorrhizal Fungi Colonies 
During the grow period, pictures were taken through the transparent containers of what 
could have been mycorrhizal colonies in containers #0, #2, and #10. At the conclusion of the 
grow period, each plant was carefully removed from the growing medium so that the roots could 
be observed. If there were any mycorrhizal fungi colonies, the process of removing the plants

26 
Discussion and Conclusions 
Overall Plant Health 
Plants grown in 100% regolith. 
Even though all plants showed some signs of distress through yellowing, drying, and 
dropping of the bottom most leaves, this was most apparent in the specimens grown in 100% 
regolith. By the end of the grow period the oldest plants in Container #1 that had sprouted in 
Trial 1 and were maintained looked almost dead when the initial fruit was harvested. After the 
fruit was harvested, the plants put out fresh new growth and one put out an additional bud by 
Day 70. This bud was not allowed to mature because it was at the end of the growing period. 
The root structures of specimens grown in 100% regolith did not appear to go deeper than 
about 2 inches in the growing medium, presumably because the regolith was too dense. 
 
 
Figure 16: Plants grown in 100% regolith without and with algae feedings

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
27 
Plants grown in mediums containing Hypnum moss. 
Plants grown with some percentage of Hypnum moss in the growing medium also 
exhibited signs of distress in the form of leaves yellowing and dropping, but not to the extent of 
the plants grown in 100% regolith simulant. There was no observable difference in the overall 
health of the plants grown in 15% and 45% moss mediums. 
The root structures of the plants grown in 15% moss mediums took longer to penetrate all 
the way to the bottoms of the growing containers, but all did eventually have roots that could be 
observed through the container bottoms. The root structures of the plants grown in 45% moss 
mediums were the quickest to have observable roots through the bottom of the containers and 
appeared to have the largest and healthiest root structures compared to the plants grown in 100% 
regolith and 15% moss. At the conclusion of the growing period when the plants were removed 
from the growing mediums, in the containers containing 45% moss, it was impossible to separate 
the plant roots from each other and the moss without significant damage. Figure 17 shows 
pictures of the plants grown in the mediums containing moss. 
 
 
Figure 17: Pictures of Plants Grown in Mediums Containing Moss

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
28 
Effectiveness of Spirulina. 
It was concluded that concentrations greater than 5% Spirulina algae in a growing 
medium prevented germination of seeds and was likely toxic. Conversely, small amounts of 
algae used for nutrition might be beneficial, but more than what was used in Trial 2 would be 
needed to be conclusive as no benefit was observed from using the algae as a nutrition source for 
some plants. 
Effectiveness of Hypnum moss. 
While there were no observable correlations to percentage of moss in growing mediums 
compared to water usage, plant health, number of fruits, or number of developed seeds during the 
growth period, there was a noticeable benefit to early and overall root spread. 
Effectiveness of Microbials used. 
Rhizobia colonies were established in the roots of all plants. Similar to using cover crops 
on Earth, this is promising for the possibility of naturally transforming the nitrogen composition 
of lunar regolith. 
There were no confirmed large colonies of mycorrhizal fungi observed and was no 
observable benefit to the plants that were inoculated with the mycorrhizal fungi. 
 
Further Studies of Interest 
Use of Spirulina. 
1. More frequent use of a low concentration of spirulina algae in suspension may 
provide a complete nutrition source for plants. Further studies to dial in a beneficial 
percentage range could be pursued. 
Use of Hypnum moss. 
2. Use of Hypnum moss did have an observable benefit to root spread in the 
experimental plants. Engineering a compact growing system to explore the 
cultivation of Hypnum or other mosses for this purpose would further explore the 
feasibility of taking transportation-efficient growable regolith amendments. 
Use of Microbials. 
3. Further study of the Rhizobia bacteria is needed to understand the rate, if any, the 
rhizobia can transform nitrogen gas into forms absorbable to plants. Future

GROWTH EXPERIMENTS OF PISUM SATIVUM IN LUNAR REGOLITH SIMULANT 
29 
experiments using Rhizobia as a variable to compare the health of plants with and 
without Rhizobium would further this understanding. 
4. Further experimentation of using the bacteria that infected these plant roots in next-
generation planting would be useful in studying the long-term viability of using 
Rhizobium in a closed-loop system. 
5. Using equipment that can analyze the nitrogen content of growing mediums 
composition of lunar regolith would also lead to more conclusive comparative results. 
6. Further experimentation with mycorrhizal fungi would be useful to understand why 
the mycorrhizal fungi colonies did not appear to thrive in these regolith mediums.
